CHAIR ( Senator Darmanin ): I declare open this hearing of the Senate Economics Legislation Committee. I begin by acknowledging the traditional custodians of the land on which we meet today and pay my respects to their elders, past and present. I extend that respect to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples here today. The committee is due to report to the Senate on Tuesday 31 March 2026. The committee has set 20 February 2026 as the date by which senators are to submit written questions on notice and 10 April 2026 as the date for the return of answers to questions taken on notice for today's proceedings.

Under standing order 26, the committee must take all evidence in public session. This includes answers to questions on notice. I remind all witnesses that, in giving evidence to the committee, they are protected by parliamentary privilege. It is unlawful for anyone to threaten or disadvantage a witness on account of evidence given to a committee, and such action may be treated by the Senate as a contempt. It is also a contempt to give false or misleading evidence.

The Senate has endorsed the following test of relevance of questions at estimates hearings. Any questions going to the operations or financial positions of the departments and agencies which are seeking funds in estimates are relevant questions for the purpose of estimates hearings. I remind officers that the Senate has resolved that there are no areas in connection with the expenditure of public funds where any person has a discretion to withhold details or explanations from the parliament or its committees unless the parliament has expressly provided otherwise.

The Senate has resolved also that an officer of a department of the Commonwealth shall not be asked to give opinions on matters of policy and shall be given reasonable opportunity to refer questions asked of the officer to superior officers or to a minister. This resolution does not preclude questions asking for explanations of policy or factual questions about when and how policies were adopted. Witnesses are reminded of the Senate order specifying the process by which a claim of public interest immunity should be raised. I incorporate the public interest immunity statement into the Hansard.

The extract read as follows—

Public interest immunity claims

That the Senate—

(a) notes that ministers and officers have continued to refuse to provide information to Senate committees without properly raising claims of public interest immunity as required by past resolutions of the Senate;

(b) reaffirms the principles of past resolutions of the Senate by this order, to provide ministers and officers with guidance as to the proper process for raising public interest immunity claims and to consolidate those past resolutions of the Senate;

(c) orders that the following operate as an order of continuing effect:

   (1) If:

(a) a Senate committee, or a senator in the course of proceedings of a committee, requests information or a document from a Commonwealth department or agency; and

(b) an officer of the department or agency to whom the request is directed believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the officer shall state to the committee the ground on which the officer believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, and specify the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

   (2) If, after receiving the officer's statement under paragraph (1), the committee or the senator requests the officer to refer the question of the disclosure of the information or document to a responsible minister, the officer shall refer that question to the minister.

   (3) If a minister, on a reference by an officer under paragraph (2), concludes that it would not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the minister shall provide to the committee a statement of the ground for that conclusion, specifying the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

   (4) A minister, in a statement under paragraph (3), shall indicate whether the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee could result only from the publication of the information or document by the committee, or could result, equally or in part, from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee as in camera evidence.

   (5) If, after considering a statement by a minister provided under paragraph (3), the committee concludes that the statement does not sufficiently justify the withholding of the information or document from the committee, the committee shall report the matter to the Senate.

   (6) A decision by a committee not to report a matter to the Senate under paragraph (5) does not prevent a senator from raising the matter in the Senate in accordance with other procedures of the Senate.

   (7) A statement that information or a document is not published, or is confidential, or consists of advice to, or internal deliberations of, government, in the absence of specification of the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document, is not a statement that meets the requirements of paragraph (1) or (4).

   (8) If a minister concludes that a statement under paragraph (3) should more appropriately be made by the head of an agency, by reason of the independence of that agency from ministerial direction or control, the minister shall inform the committee of that conclusion and the reason for that conclusion, and shall refer the matter to the head of the agency, who shall then be required to provide a statement in accordance with paragraph (3).

(d) requires the Procedure Committee to review the operation of this order and report to the

Senate by 20 August 2009.

(13 May 2009 J.1941)

CHAIR: I remind senators of their obligations under the Behaviour Code for Australian Parliamentarians to treat witnesses with dignity, courtesy, fairness and respect.

Reserve Bank of Australia

[09:03]

CHAIR: The committee welcomes the Reserve Bank of Australia and its representatives, Governor Michele Bullock and Assistant Governor Dr Christopher Kent. Would you like to make an opening statement, Ms Bullock?

Ms Bullock : No.

CHAIR: We will go straight to questions then. I will kick off quickly. We met not very long ago, in December. What are some of the key points around what has really changed since the last time we spoke in December?

Ms Bullock : A few things have changed. You recall that, when we last spoke in September, we'd highlighted that we'd had a run of news that was, really, all suggesting that inflation risks on the upside were increasing, and we were seeing demand come in a bit stronger than expected. We were seeing the labour market holding up a bit stronger than expected. Inflation numbers were coming in a bit higher than expected. The world economy actually recovered a lot more than people thought it would. There was a lot of pessimism earlier in the year about that. All of these things were adding to inflationary pressures. As you will see, news from December to now has just reinforced all of that. The board took the view, at its meeting last week, that inflation running at something with a three in front of it was not acceptable. It's not in the range, and it's not forecast to get back into the range for another couple of years. So the appropriate response to these changing circumstances was to raise the interest rate.

CHAIR: Can you talk a bit about private demand and how that has changed in your observations since we last spoke—I remember asking a little bit about that last time, what you'd seen then—and what's happened since then.

Ms Bullock : Private demand did come in stronger than expected. It's both consumption and investment. Now some of that investment is in lumpy things like data centres, for example—which is one people have highlighted. It's lumpy. It's also quite import intense, so it doesn't necessarily add to pressure on domestic production. Nevertheless, it was indicative, along with the consumption indicators, that people were getting out and consuming. It's a little bit difficult because seasonal patterns have changed a bit, particularly with the advent of Black Friday sales and those sorts of things, so there is a sense in which we've got to be a little bit careful because some of it is bringing consumption forward to take advantage of those sorts of sales. So we're alert to that.

Notwithstanding that, we did see more strength in consumption than we were expecting, and that's reflecting, really, the recovery in real incomes over the last year. I think the real disposable household incomes have been rising, and that's being reflected in consumption. Consumption and investment have surprised us on the upside, and we think that's partly what's driving inflation.

The other point I would make is that the board and the staff have reassessed where we think we are in terms of balancing the economy. We thought we were close to balance between supply and demand. We've reassessed that. You will see in our recent Statement on monetary policy that we now assess that actually we are in a situation of excess demand, the labour market remains tight and these two things are keeping pressure on inflation.

CHAIR: So, just in terms of the kind of investment comments you made then, things can be a bit lumpy. What would you say about the energy transition in terms of the recent pick-up in private investment outside of data centres?

Ms Bullock : I think that's also partly being reflected in the investment figures. Again, that is also lumpy and it's also import intensive. But that's certainly part of the explanation.

CHAIR: Yes. And could we very quickly have just a couple of comments from you about the ever-present geopolitical instability and political uncertainty. You said—and I've heard this commentary already—that the global outlook was better than was anticipated. What are you seeing now in terms of the impact on the Australian economy? Could you also make a comment, independent of tariffs, on some of the risks to the Chinese economy, and do you have any thoughts about the outcome of the recent Japanese election?

Ms Bullock : Oh, okay.

CHAIR: Sorry! That will be my last question.

Ms Bullock : What I'm going to do is talk a little bit about it and then pass to Chris Kent to talk a little bit about financial markets, because I think that's an important part of the story.

Yes, geopolitical risks are heightened. When you go back to May last year, there was a lot of pessimism about the world economy. Everyone was marking down their forecasts for the world economy. That was based on the fact that there were massive tariffs being threatened. There were concerns that not only the US would impose tariffs but also other countries would retaliate with their own tariffs. Everyone revised down their forecasts for growth, and there were concerns that the global trading system, basically, would freeze up. None of that ended up happening. And, in fact, if you look now at everyone's forecasts, they not only are revised back up but are above where they were prior to being revised down.

I think a couple of things have happened. First of all, the tariffs haven't turned out to be as bad as everyone thought they would be. The US tariffs are certainly higher than they were prior to the April announcements, but the effective tariff rate is actually a little bit lower than that because there are lots of exemptions. So that's partly it.

The second thing is that the global trading system has actually responded pretty quickly and effectively. Chinese exports to the US are down, but they've increased in other areas. In particular, the AI boom has really driven great exports for the East Asian countries. I'm thinking of Korea and Taiwan in particular. That's driven really strong growth there, so that's been really helpful for us. So that's that. However, there is this constant uncertainty and geopolitical setting there. Where you might think that might start to bite is the financial markets, so I'm going to let Chris say a few things about that.

Dr Kent : Sure. I think that's right. And we've seen from time to time, when geopolitical tensions of one sort or another have spiked, some response of financial markets. I think, overall, though, that's not been that enduring, partly because threats, for example, of the US taking over Greenland have been stepped back. Threats of additional tariffs from the US on Europe because of that dispute over Greenland have been pulled back. So markets have been disrupted for a time but then pulled back, partly because the geopolitical tensions have eased.

I think the thing that is surprising in some ways, though, but is a reflection of what the governor was saying in terms of the global economy being better, is that financial markets valuations remain quite elevated—equity prices, for example. Generally, people aren't asking when they're investing for higher returns—another way of saying that is that they're happy with pretty low returns for the risk that they might be taking.

Having said that, there are some effects; longer term, we're seeing term premia. When governments borrow at very long term—in Japan or in the US, particularly—they're paying a little bit of a premium that they weren't paying in the past. And that's because of concerns about the sustainability of very large deficits and debt, and that comes around to the Japanese election. There has been concern that that's going to be a bit stimulatory, which will be inflationary and push up the cost of them borrowing. But, all in all, financial markets are taking it in their stride, and financial conditions are quite favourable, including for Australian companies and Australian banks raising funding offshore.

CHAIR: I will pass to Senator Hume.

Senator HUME: Just on that issue of global volatility—obviously, if one of your measures for global volatility is the VIX index, it does seem to have come back down since the beginning of the year, which would suggest then that domestic factors are more at play in decisions that the board are making now than international factors.

Ms Bullock : I think that's probably fair to say at the moment. The focus for the board has been on domestic inflation. Through the second half of last year, increasingly from September on, not only we but the markets were starting to focus on the domestic factors which were suggesting inflationary pressures were rising, and that happened progressively. It didn't happen all of a sudden; it had been happening progressively since September as more and more data became available. It's not just us. We were changing our view, but the market was also changing its view. I think that's important.

Dr Kent : I think that's right, but global developments had an effect on our domestic financial conditions. As I just suggested, equity prices relatively elevated the cost of borrowing, including of issuing bonds offshore by banks in Australia, for example. Large Australian companies are pretty low, and funding is readily available. That means financial conditions from the global side of things are easier than they otherwise might be.

Senator HUME: Okay, that's good. Thank you. I have no intention of prosecuting any of the discussions that went; obviously, you appeared before the House economics committee last week, and we don't want to make you repeat yourselves. But I did notice, in your press conference following the most recent rate rise, that you responded, Governor, to a question on four occasions by saying that you don't comment on fiscal policy, that fiscal policy is not your business and that we work with what we've got. I perfectly understand that, but I want to just unpack that a little bit. Is it right, then, to interpret this as the RBA having a general policy of not commenting on fiscal policy?

Ms Bullock : I don't believe that our job is to tell the government or the parliament what to do with fiscal policy. That is a matter—fiscal policy, as I've said on a number of occasions, is about providing goods and services and infrastructure for the Australian economy. That is the purview of the parliament and the government. It is not the Reserve Bank's role to comment on what governments and parliaments should be doing and where they should be spending their money.

Senator HUME: I understand exactly the position you're coming from. However, it is also fair to say that fiscal policy can be a driver of inflation. It can have a significant impact on inflation, even if you don't comment about it.

Ms Bullock : It can. As I said at the House of Representatives last week, it is a part of aggregate demand. And, if you're in a situation like we are at the moment, where we have excess demand, private and public are both part of demand.

Senator HUME: Yes.

Ms Bullock : So, yes, mathematically, it is a fact that that is the case.

Senator HUME: I just want to be very clear on this. As a general rule, the RBA does not comment on fiscal policy, but it is wrong to assume that, just because the RBA hasn't mentioned fiscal policy or doesn't comment on fiscal policy, it didn't have an effect on your decision, because it does contribute to aggregate demand, as you say, which is something that the RBA bases its decisions on?

Ms Bullock : If you're talking about our most recent decision, our most recent decision was based on the fact that aggregate demand is, we think, in excess of the ability of the economy to supply those goods and services. Both public and private contribute to that. But what I would say is that, if you look at the difference between our forecasts in November, where we had inflation coming back into the band, and our forecasts now, where inflation isn't, the key difference there is not fiscal policy. It's pretty much the same as it was in November. The key difference is private demand.

Senator HUME: Yes. Okay. I hear you, and I've got some questions about that. I suppose what I'm trying to understand is that—the Treasurer said that fiscal policy was not a factor in the decision that you took. Clearly, that is not the case. Just because you don't talk about fiscal policy doesn't mean you endorse fiscal policy. That would be an awkward position to be in, wouldn't it?

Ms Bullock : We don't endorse, we don't advocate, we don't do anything for fiscal policy.

Senator HUME: So it's reasonable to conclude that, on the basis of the fact that it wasn't mentioned in the accompanying release that government spending has no bearing on your decision-making, of course it does, because of its contribution to aggregate demand.

Ms Bullock : Yes, and I've said that before, and I have nothing more to add on that.

Senator HUME: Thank you. I want to refer you to page 27 of the February Statement on monetary policy. I have a copy of that in front of me. I can share one with the committee if you would like, but I'm sure you have one yourself.

Ms Bullock : Page 27?

Senator HUME: Yes. There is a line in the section of text on the bottom left-hand side of that page. I will read it to you. It says:

Budget estimates of the fiscal balance provide a more comprehensive view of developments in fiscal policy than public demand alone.

My interpretation of that is that the role of public demand significantly understates the role of government spending in driving aggregate demand and inflation. Is that right?

Ms Bullock : I don't know if I'd add 'significantly' in there. What I'd say is that, yes, we know that what public demand is defined as doesn't incorporate other things that governments spend money on. Particularly, I'm thinking about transfers and that sort of—JobSeeker, for example, or pensions and those sorts of things. Those sorts of things go directly to people, and then they can go out and spend them. So there's a sense in which spending and transfers can add to private demand, because they put money in people's pockets.

Senator HUME: Right. Okay. That's what I wanted to understand. Private demand can actually contain a whole bunch of government spending. If government is spending on—and I'm going to pull something out of the air—childcare subsidies or electricity subsidies, or whatever it might be, that can contribute to private demand.

Ms Bullock : My understanding is that those sorts of subsidies are in public demand; they're not in the transfers bucket. But, yes, to the extent that people get an electricity subsidy, they don't have to spend that money on electricity. That potentially frees up money for them to spend on other things.

Senator HUME: So public demand excludes transfers, but, when they're spent, they show up in private demand?

Ms Bullock : If they're spent. It depends on what people do with the money that they either get in direct transfers or the additional space they get in their income, if you like, because they're getting other things subsidised. It depends what people do with that, and different segments of the community have different marginal propensities to consume. People on lower incomes, you might expect, would spend most of it because they're often constrained. People on higher incomes may not.

Senator HUME: Is it then also true that there is a multiplier effect from public demand—when public demand increases, there's a multiplier effect that boosts private demand as well?

Ms Bullock : Yes, there are multiplier effects in demand.

Senator HUME: So the bottom line is public demand significantly understates the inflationary impact of government spending.

Ms Bullock : I don't know if I'd put it quite like that, because it depends where you are in the cycle in these things. If, for example, you were in a private sector downturn, then public demand, cyclically, you would expect often—if you've got, say, unemployment rising in a recession or something, that would usually result in more public spending on unemployment benefits, and that's what helps to stabilise the economy.

Senator HUME: I understand that. Is it then correct to conclude that, if public demand is making a smaller contribution to GDP growth over time, that doesn't, in and of itself, imply anything definitive about the effect of government spending and the impact that it's having on inflation. Is that right?

Ms Bullock : It depends on where you are in the cycle, and, at the moment, where we are in the cycle is excess demand. If you are in a period of excess supply, which some countries are at the moment, in fact, then more demand from the public doesn't necessarily add to inflationary pressures. That's all I'm saying.

Senator HUME: What about now, when the economy is above its potential?

Ms Bullock : At the moment, when the economy is above its potential and when demand is above its potential, both public and private demand are contributing to demand being above supply. I have said this a number of times. I really don't think I have anything more to add.

Senator HUME: All other things being equal, if the budget bottom line deteriorates by—let me take a step back. If we talk about just government spending, which you've identified as a more comprehensive measure, in the past two financial years, 2023-24 and 2025-26, the budget bottom line has deteriorated by 1.9 percentage points of GDP, of which 1.8 percentage points is due to higher spending. Does that mean that, if all other things were equal, the budget bottom line deteriorates by 1.9 percentage points of GDP? Does that raise aggregate demand and then push up inflation?

Ms Bullock : Look, I really don't think I have anything more to add on this. I answered this question all last week. I answered it at the press conference. I answered it at House of Reps on multitude of occasions. When we look at what to do with monetary policy, we look at aggregate demand, incorporating public and private, and we take public as given, including public spending, and we set interest rates accordingly. As I said at the moment, with the total demand, we think it's above the ability of the economy to supply those, and that's why we're exhibiting inflation.

Senator HUME: I want to refer you to the statement that you put out following the December meeting of the Monetary Policy Board. That was really the first time the RBA sounded the alarm about inflation re-emerging.

Ms Bullock : No, that wasn't. We were sounding the alarm earlier than that. In fact—

Senator HUME: When did you sound the alarm that inflation was re-emerging?

Ms Bullock : We were sounding the alarm back in September. Certainly, in our November Statement on monetary policy, we were following that up with concerns about inflationary risks on the upside. So, no, it's not fair to say that December was the first time we were alert to this.

Senator HUME: The reason why I ask is that the release in December doesn't mention government spending. It doesn't mention public demand.

Ms Bullock : No.

Senator HUME: But it mentions private demand or the private sector twice. It says:

Economic activity continues to recover. Growth in private demand has strengthened, driven by both consumption and investment.

Now, this meeting was held just a few days after the release of the September national accounts, so I presume that the information that was in the national accounts was part of the evidence that the board considered?

Ms Bullock : Yes.

Senator HUME: Fantastic. Can I just refer you to some figures for public and private demand that were released as part of the September national accounts. I'm particularly interested in the growth rates of each. I have a screenshot—it's a bit bizarre, but it is the ABS spreadsheet from national accounts, which I can share with you there. You have to dig quite deep to find this, but I'm sure that the RBA has considered it. In the September quarter, was it private demand or public demand that was growing faster?

Ms Bullock : The contribution to GDP growth in the September quarter was predominantly private.

Senator HUME: It was private.

Ms Bullock : And you can see that, if you look at our Statement on monetary policy from February; if you go to graph 2.6, it shows you GDP growth, with contributions, and you can see that the contribution of public demand in that quarter was not the predominant contribution to GDP growth; it was private demand.

Senator HUME: I know that the Treasurer has referred to this, but I wasn't necessarily talking about the contribution; I was talking about the growth rate, as opposed to the contribution.

Ms Bullock : Well, yes—everything's growing. The economy is growing, and what we're saying is what was the main contribution to that growth. So public demand was growing, yes, and private demand was growing.

Senator HUME: But you'd hope that the contribution of private demand was greater. I mean, it's a bigger share of the economy, hopefully, in a healthy economy.

Ms Bullock : It is a bigger share of the economy. Private is a bigger share of the economy.

Senator HUME: Yes. So of course it's going to make a bigger contribution.

Ms Bullock : Both of them are growing, and what surprised us, in that September quarter release, was the strength of the private part. That's what surprised us.

Senator HUME: If public and private demand are growing at the same rate, then they're putting a similar proportionate degree of pressure on aggregate demand—can we take that as a given, all other things being equal?

Ms Bullock : If they're both growing at the same rate and they're both growing above the supply capacity of the economy, then they're both contributing to excess demand. I really feel that I am answering the same question over and over again.

Senator HUME: I understand that you must feel that, Governor, but it's because we need to be able to understand what it is that's driving your decision, that's obviously—

Ms Bullock : And I—

Senator HUME: You know that Australians are very disappointed to find that there's a 13th interest rate rise under this government. People were hanging on your words, like some sort of internet influencer, last week. So this is really important—to understand what it is that's driving the decisions that you're having to take.

Ms Bullock : And I've told you, what is driving the decision is that we have a situation where there is excess demand. We don't attribute it to private and public, but total demand is above the ability of the economy to provide those goods and services. That means there's inflationary pressure, and it's taking too long to get inflation back down. I understand people are disappointed with the interest rate rise, but it would not be appropriate, in the circumstances we've got, to not take that action, because inflation is bad for everyone. It is bad particularly for people on lower incomes, and it's bad for mortgagees as well as for people who own their own homes. High inflation is bad, and we've seen that over the past few years. That's what's driving the decision of the board—to make sure that we can not let inflation get away and we can bring it back down to target.

Senator HUME: I couldn't agree with you more, Ms Bullock, and can I tell you that, I think, from everybody around this table, we agree that inflation is bad. The question is what it is that a government can do to help you, to make sure that you don't have to raise interest rates again.

Ms Bullock : That is for the government to decide. It is not for me to tell the government what to do.

Senator HUME: Exactly, and that's exactly what we're trying to help them do.

Ms Bullock : Okay.

Dr Kent : The point you made in the statement that you referred to, the Statement on monetary policy, about the fiscal balance—there's also the other side of the ledger, the revenue side. Most importantly, there are the states. The states make a significant contribution to both spending and taxation.

CHAIR: I'm going to have to rotate the call. I'll go to Senator McKim for 15 minutes, and then we will rotate around in 10-minute blocks.

Senator McKIM: Thanks very much for coming in, and good morning to you both. Ms Bullock, in your public remarks post the board meeting last week, I was particularly interested that you singled out credit growth as one of the factors that concerned you and the board. We're receiving a rolling series of lending figures at the moment. Yesterday we received lending figures around the annual growth in the value of credit for property investors, which jumped from 19 per cent in the September quarter to 32 per cent in the last three months of the year.

Ms Bullock : Growth in lending to—

Senator McKIM: Growth in the value of lending for property investors.

Dr Kent : It must be new lending growth.

Ms Bullock : Is that what you're talking about—new lending growth?

Senator McKIM: Yes, it is. Can you quantify the contribution that that particular pretty large spike in lending makes to the overall credit growth that you identified as a concern to the board, and is a 32 per cent annual growth in new lending for property investors sustainable?

Ms Bullock : Chris, do you want to talk a little bit about credit growth?

Dr Kent : So you're talking about the growth in the flow of new lending—

Ms Bullock : Which is a different thing to what—

Dr Kent : which then comes in to affect the stock.

Senator McKIM: I'm asking, firstly, whether that contributes to the credit growth that you identified.

Ms Bullock : Yes, it does.

Dr Kent : Absolutely, yes. It's a significant contribution.

Senator McKIM: Secondly, is that sustainable? That's a large spike. Is that sustainable, and what are the factors that are driving that? More broadly, what are the factors that are driving the credit growth that you identified as one of your concerns?

Ms Bullock : I'll make a couple of remarks and then let Chris talk specifically about credit growth. We know that when interest rates decline and housing prices are rising, investors respond much more quickly than owner-occupiers. Owner-occupiers, I think, still account for more than investor credit does—I think that's fair to say, isn't it, Chris?

Dr Kent : Yes.

Ms Bullock : But what we've observed is that, over recent times, investor credit growth has been well above average in the last year or so. Owner-occupier credit has been picking up, but it's been around average or maybe a little bit below. A lot of the strength in credit has been driven by investor credit.

Senator McKIM: What are the factors that are driving that?

Ms Bullock : Two things. One is slightly lower interest rates. It started to pick up before interest rates came down, so it probably was anticipation of lower interest rates. The second thing is that, as I said earlier, investors tend to move with the housing price cycle. When housing prices are going up, investors tend to be more in the market, and, when they're coming down, they're generally pulling back a bit. There's one point worth making here. From a financial stability perspective, we watch this because there is a possibility for investor behaviour to exacerbate cycles. That potentially might have financial stability implications if, for example, the cycle turns and the investors pull out. That exacerbates the downturn, and that might have implications for other borrowers.

Senator McKIM: Do government policy settings like the capital gains tax discount or the five per cent deposit scheme have an impact on investor behaviour and therefore the spike that we've seen in lending to property investors recently?

Ms Bullock : The five per cent deposit scheme applies to first home buyers. Some of them may be investors—I don't know—but a lot of them probably aren't. A lot of them are probably just trying to get in.

Senator McKIM: But do you think that investors might anticipate an increase in demand from first home buyers and therefore decide to jump into the market?

Ms Bullock : They may. That's possible.

Dr Kent : That may be about them shifting. If they're ready to go with their finance—if they're ready to buy—they might think, 'If I can move a bit faster at the margin, I'll come in earlier.' But at the same time, when they show up at auctions, there are going to be more first home buyers that would be willing to compete with them. So it's sort of double edged.

Ms Bullock : And then, on the taxation side of things, the point here is that it has, as far as I can tell, been basically steady. The first home buyer scheme is new but the taxation things you refer to haven't changed, so they're not driving or adding to anything in the current cycle. They are just things that have been constant underneath.

Senator McKIM: Thanks. With that spike that we're discussing, for example, Westpac have said that 39 per cent of all lending is for property investors at the moment. That's the highest share, by the way, since 2017. Does that pose any financial system risk issues to you or raise any inflationary concerns?

Ms Bullock : It doesn't. We obviously are alert to the potential financial stability implications, and part of the reason for APRA putting its recent guardrails on debt-to-income ratios was to be a bit forward looking in this sense—to say, basically, 'These are the guardrails, so be careful if you start to approach those guardrails, because we're worried that there are possible vulnerabilities building up in the system.' Our most recent Financial stability review looked at all of this. It always looks at these sorts of things. We don't see financial stability as being a problem at the moment.

Senator McKIM: Okay. Thanks. This is my last question on this. Ninety-two per cent of credit to property investors is put into the existing housing stock as opposed to new builds. Do you think this contributes anything to the productivity challenge that we have in Australia at the moment?

Ms Bullock : I'm not really sure in what way. I mean—

Senator McKIM: Well, it's not generating productive investment into new houses, for example. It's simply driving property speculation into the existing housing stock.

Ms Bullock : Well, you've also got to remember that the rental stock in Australia is owned by the households, the very investors you're talking about. In other countries, this isn't necessarily the case. A lot of the rental stock is owned by corporations or by super funds. In Australia, the rental stock is owned basically by other households. So there are two sides to this coin; that is the only point I'm making. As to the way that investors choose to buy established housing or new housing, I don't know why that might be the case. It might be that there are certain advantages taxation-wise for doing that. But again, with all these things, the whole housing market issue basically comes down to a supply and demand story. As we've talked about before, we aren't building enough houses and demand for houses obviously is outstripping that. That's what's driving not only the housing prices issue but also the rental situation and vacancy rates.

Dr Kent : The other thing to remember, of course, is that an investor might be buying from another investor who's already paid off their loan, and they did that as part of a retirement strategy, and they're going to use those funds to fund their retirement.

Senator McKIM: Thanks. You've been very clear, Ms Bullock, that you understand that millions of Australians are doing it really tough at the moment, and that's clearly what I'm hearing. I hear from a lot of people—I'm sure you do too—about how hard it is at the moment. A lot of people feel like they're working harder and harder but still falling further and further behind in the daily or weekly or monthly financial grind that they're facing. They feel that their living standards are actually declining or that they're having to work harder just to maintain the same standard of living, and there's a large sense of frustration in large parts of the community about that.

It really caught my eye that we're now seeing corporate profit forecasts revised significantly upwards. This week UBS released a forecast of ASX200 corporate profits that went up from a three per cent forecast to a 12 per cent forecast. What's causing this two-phase economy, where corporate profits are really, really strong and look like they're going to grow significantly over the next 12 months, and yet so many millions of Australians are really struggling at the moment? It's a genuine question. How are we in such a two-speed economy, where some people are doing so well, the big corporates are doing so well and people at the bottom feel like they're working harder and harder and can't get ahead?

Ms Bullock : What people are observing is that the price level has risen substantially over the last few years. That has meant that, when everyone goes to the supermarket now, they just look at the prices and they remember they were here and now they're 20 per cent higher, and that hurts people. It's also true to say that, as always, there is a range of different experiences across the economy. You have some people on relatively low incomes. You have some people on higher incomes.

The reason that corporates can do well at the moment comes back again to the point that, in total, there is excess demand for goods and services in the economy. Not everyone is contributing to that, but there is excess demand. In those circumstances, businesses make money. They can put up their prices. They can recover their costs. We know that unit labour costs are still rising by quite a lot. To the extent that there is demand for their goods and services, businesses can put up their prices to account for that and for the rising cost of their inputs. So, yes, there is always a range of experience across the economy.

From my perspective and that of monetary policy—and I've said this before—we recognise that interest rates have differential effects on different parts of the economy. That's just the way monetary policy works. Unfortunately, when interest rates are going up, it hurts people that have debt. When interest rates are going down, the people getting hurt are the people that actually have savings. It has differential effects. We know that. That's monetary policy.

Dr Kent : I wouldn't overstate this, but there's also a global dimension because this is a common feature. One aspect that impinges on us is commodity prices. A lot of the listed corporates, which UBS would, I assume, be referring to, are profiting off higher commodity prices, which is a global phenomenon that is, in the main, to the benefit of the Australian economy. That doesn't mean that households who are struggling to make ends meet won't be adversely affected at the margin by higher prices of, say, the food in the shops that relates to that. But, often, the cost of beef to the farmer is a small share of what the customer is paying at the store.

CHAIR: You've got two minutes, Senator McKim.

Senator McKIM: Thanks to you both. That's really helpful. I've got two more questions and then I'm done. Ms Bullock, this is a question phrased in the global context, but not quite in the context that Dr Kent was just talking about. I want to ask you about the impacts of inflation on political circumstances around the world. There does appear to be a relationship between the difficulties of a lot of people with debt—which you've just acknowledged—living through an inflationary cycle and a cycle of interest rate rises and a shift to the hard right in global politics, whether that's reform in the UK, Trump in the US, the rise of the Nazi Party in the Weimar Republic at the moment, Le Pen in France or One Nation here in Australia. Have you thought about that at all? And do you have any views you'd like to share about the societal impacts of inflation rather than the economic impacts of inflation?

Ms Bullock : No, I have nothing to say on the political.

Senator McKIM: I actually thought that might be your answer, Ms Bullock. I have no truck with that answer, by the way. I have one last question. The board unanimously voted last week to increase interest rates. Obviously, you've got the Secretary to the Treasury on the board. I wanted to ask—and this is a transparency question—whether there are either formal or informal governance arrangements where the Treasury secretary is expected, in some way, to vote in the same way as the rest of the board, or does everyone on the board, including the secretary, exercise a genuinely independent vote.

Ms Bullock : Everyone on the board exercises a genuine right to have their own vote.

Senator McKIM: If that's the case, is it open for the Treasurer to give direction to the Treasury secretary to vote in a particular way or not? I ask because I know that there's a view that the RBA is apolitical, but I have a different view. I'm not suggesting you have partisan politics. I don't make that allegation at all. But the decisions you make are political decisions, in my view, because they impact on the day-to-day lived experience of all Australians, as you've said before, and they do have an impact on the political debate in this country.

Just to be clear, I'm not accusing you of making partisan decisions. I've too much respect for you and the board for that. But I wanted to ask whether there is a possibility that the Treasurer could direct the Treasury secretary and whether, in your view, that is something that is a risk or, at least, a potential risk.

Ms Bullock : I don't believe it is. The review of the Reserve Bank of Australia looked at the issue of the Treasury secretary on the board. It confirmed that they felt it remained appropriate, but they also made it extremely clear—and the government accepted this—that they are there as an individual. They are not there as a representative of the Treasurer.

CHAIR: Senator Sharma.

Senator SHARMA: Good morning, Ms Bullock and Dr Kent. I had some questions about the table on page 4 of the February Statement on monetary policy.

Ms Bullock : Page 4?

Senator SHARMA: Yes. I believe it's the overview table. As I understand it, based on your latest forecasts, even with an additional one to two rate increases because they're priced in, you don't quite get back to the midpoint of the target band for inflation within the 2½-year horizon. That's correct?

Ms Bullock : That's what that says, yes, because 2.5 is the midpoint of the target.

Senator SHARMA: Am I reading this right? You've got the cash rate also going to 4.2 at the end of the forecast period. It's currently 3.85. So that's a 35 basis point increase.

Ms Bullock : Yes, that's a technical assumption.

Senator SHARMA: Okay. If you assume that the cash rate goes up, we still won't get back to the inflation midpoint.

Ms Bullock : That's what the central forecast says.

Senator SHARMA: Okay. On the GDP forecasts, I noticed that there's been a significant downgrade of those—at least if you get beyond the middle of this year. They're down to 1.6 per cent.

Ms Bullock : There's been an upgrade in the near term, and then a downgrade in the out year, which reflects the higher interest rate profile and the higher exchange rate.

Senator SHARMA: I read this somewhere, so I just wanted to check. Is 1.6 the slowest growth at the end of a forecasting horizon that the RBA produces?

Ms Bullock : I don't believe it is. I think our November 2022 forecasts had a lower growth rate than that.

Senator SHARMA: But it's pretty low outside a recession.

Ms Bullock : It's pretty low outside of a recession.

Senator SHARMA: You touched on this earlier, but what were the drivers in your forecasting framework that have driven that downgrade? You mentioned the exchange rate—

Ms Bullock : There are two things that have changed between the November forecasts and here. The main things that are driving this different profile are the stronger near term—as I said, we were surprised on the upside on a few things—and the higher cash rate path and the higher exchange rate. The higher exchange rate also tightens things up and puts downward pressure on inflation and the economy. Those two things are helping to drive the growth rate back down again, below the rate of growth of supply. Again, as I said earlier, we've got a situation where we've got excess demand, and that's what helps to close the gap and bring inflation back down into the band.

Senator SHARMA: In my layperson's understanding, we've got the economy growing in, say, December 2027 at 1.6 per cent but trimmed mean inflation still outside the target band. That suggests to me that the speed limit in the economy now is below two per cent—the economy can't grow.

Ms Bullock : Those are our productivity assumptions for the short term for the period we forecast. Productivity is only growing by about 0.7 per cent, I think, in our forecasts, which means that, yes, the supply side of the economy is probably only growing by about two per cent. That's part of the challenge. Unless we can improve productivity, we're going to find it hard to grow much more than two per cent a year without having inflationary issues.

Senator SHARMA: Right, I understand. Unless we can get productivity above 0.7 per cent, which is your long-range forecast—

Ms Bullock : That's not our long-run forecast; it's our short run. It's not really a forecast. It's an assumption, based on what we've been observing in terms of actual productivity outcomes plus, quite frankly, the inflation and the unit labour cost outcomes.

Senator SHARMA: So unless we can get productivity moving higher, though, the growth rate is likely to stay at around two per cent.

Ms Bullock : Productivity is all about producing more with the same amount of labour and capital. That's what raises living standards. If you can't get productivity increasing more quickly, then you can't grow the economy and you can't raise living standards as quickly.

Senator SHARMA: Historically, there's been a difference in the productivity performance between the public sector and the private sector, right?

Ms Bullock : Yes, but I think there are differences not only between the public and the private sectors but between different sectors of the economy. There are actually massive differences in productivity, in levels and in growth rates—

Dr Kent : And in the ability to measure it accurately.

Ms Bullock : That was the other point.

Senator SHARMA: Is there some truth in the view that, because the lower productivity sectors of the economy have been growing more quickly than the more productive parts—that's predominantly public sector rather than private sector—our overall productivity performance has declined?

Ms Bullock : Our analysis actually doesn't suggest that that is the main part of what's going on. There is some impact of that. There is a measurement issue, as Chris was referring to, in that, for many parts, particularly of the non-market service area—I'm thinking about things like health care, aged care and those sorts of areas, which we have seen growth in—outputs are measured by inputs, so, by definition, there is no productivity growth over time. There is no accounting for quality, so, by definition, you don't get any productivity growth.

Our analysis suggests that there's a little bit of that, but that's not the main game. You only have to look overseas to see similar declines in productivity over time. The US is an exception. In most other countries productivity growth has slowed over the decades. We're no different. It's true that we have not had any productivity growth over the last 10 years, probably. The productivity level is probably about where it was pre COVID and it's had lots of big wiggles in the middle. I discourage people from looking at quarterly changes in productivity. You've got to think about it in a slightly more long-run sense. But it is concerning that it hasn't grown since pre COVID. As I said earlier, it's really important that we get productivity growth in all areas of the economy if we can. But our analysis suggests that this market/non-market thing you're referring is not the main game.

Senator SHARMA: Just to the United States, because you raised that, does the fact that they continue to have a better productivity performance mean that their economy is able to grow more quickly without triggering inflation, which is what we've seen now over the last three to four years?

Ms Bullock : Yes—although they've had an inflation problem too and they still have an inflation problem. So, yes, they have had strong productivity growth, and they're the stand-out.

Dr Kent : Yes, very much so.

Senator SHARMA: Amongst advanced economies?

Dr Kent : Yes.

Ms Bullock : Yes.

Senator SHARMA: I'm just going back to inflation and the model of the page 4 table. The assumption is that the cash rate goes up by 35 to 45 basis points but trimmed-mean inflation still remains above the midpoint of the target. Is it fair to say that we will need additional rate rises to bring trimmed-mean inflation back to the midpoint of the target, everything else being equal?

Ms Bullock : That's the central forecast. What it actually means isn't clear. It might, but it might not. I would refer you to graph 3.6 on page 53 of the statement, which gives you a fan chart showing historical errors of forecasts. The board, in its approach, is not saying that this is the rate path it's going to take. It's cautious. We saw in the middle of last year that we thought inflation was coming back into the band, and it hasn't. So forecasts are fallible. Don't read that the interest rate path we've got in there is the interest rate path we have to have. It might be, but it might not be, hence why the board say that they are going to be continually looking at the data. It tells us where we are and what that means for our forecast going forward, and we will be continually reassessing that. If we need to go up further because inflation is entrenched, the board will do so, because that is its primary mandate.

Senator SHARMA: I understand that these are forecasts, but, as I read table 4, the outlook is for growth below two per cent, inflation above the midpoint of the target band, higher interest rate rises and declining real wages out to the middle of 2028.

Ms Bullock : It's not a nice picture, but I do want to inject one positive thing here, and that is the labour market. Everyone's been focusing on the negatives, but we're in this position because the economy is actually doing okay. It can't grow really strongly because productivity is not growing, but the labour market is holding up. It's still a little bit tight, and this is good news. In fact, it's much better news than some other countries overseas have seen with their labour markets.

CHAIR: Senator Bragg.

Senator BRAGG: Thank you, Governor, for being here today. In terms of housing policy, I imagine that it's still your view that supply is the key thing.

Ms Bullock : The interaction of supply and demand is the key thing to do with housing.

Senator BRAGG: Getting the numbers up?

Ms Bullock : We have a shortage of housing. This isn't something that's just occurred overnight; it's been decades in the making.

Senator BRAGG: It is instructive, though, to look at the numbers on dwelling completions. If you go back a decade ago, to the middle of the last decade, we were getting 220,000 in some years, with an average of 200,000 per year. Now, we're back to 170,000 houses per year. This year looks like about that number. So it does appear that we are heading in the wrong direction in terms of the supply. If supply is the most important thing, and we're heading in the wrong direction, what do you think should happen?

Ms Bullock : Again, I am not the housing policy person. That is for governments. My only reflection on that is that the governments seem to making the right noises in terms of looking at ways of making it easier for developments. I think higher density is an important part of this. Certainly, when the bank talks to building companies in liaison, they say that the process of getting a higher density development approved is very, very challenging, particularly in New South Wales. I know the New South Wales government are looking at that. So governments need to look at those issues.

Senator BRAGG: I think the turn of phrase you use there is very revealing because you just said that the government seemed to be making the right noises. I would agree with—

Ms Bullock : I'm sorry; I'd go further than that. I'd say that I think, in the New South Wales government's case, they are actually making moves.

Senator BRAGG: Unfortunately, though, they're 44 per cent behind on their housing target.

Ms Bullock : Again, it's not for me. This is not my policy.

Senator O'NEILL: That's the big change.

Senator BRAGG: The target's a good idea. There's no problem with the target.

Senator O'NEILL: Yes. Exactly: you didn't have any.

Ms Bullock : Can I also add one other thing—

Senator BRAGG: Thanks for that. That's great.

Ms Bullock : and that is that—

Senator BRAGG: Thanks for that. That's very mature.

Ms Bullock : coming out of COVID—

Senator BRAGG: Sorry, I was just reflecting on the other senator's very immature comments.

CHAIR: Let's keep to the Q&A at this stage.

Senator BRAGG: Sorry, Governor.

Ms Bullock : I was going to say that, coming out of COVID, the housing construction has been quite constrained, and it's been constrained in a couple of ways. One is that we often hear that you just can't get trades.

Senator BRAGG: Yes.

Ms Bullock : Also, what we hear from our liaison is that the time taken to finish is easing somewhat, but certainly, in the year or so coming out of COVID, it actually strung out because you couldn't get these trades. There was a big backlog. They couldn't get the trades to finish them. So there are issues about development, but there are also issues about how you actually get them built.

Senator BRAGG: Yes. I think you're right. All governments—of all colours—are making the right noises. In the case of the federal government, the government's own statement is that they're spending $45 billion on housing. That's one of their main talking points. But, clearly, we are not getting the numbers up. Is the solution here to spend more money? What else could the federal government do to get the numbers up?

Ms Bullock : I am not a housing policy person. I cannot decide what I think the government should do on these matters. It is a knotty problem.

Senator BRAGG: Fair enough. Let's just stick to your figures then. I am looking at the statement of monetary policy projections on dwelling investment. Your November 2025 dwelling investment projections had it going from 4.8 per cent growth in December 2025 through to 2.5 per cent growth in December 2027.

Ms Bullock : Is this the November statement or the February statement.

Senator BRAGG: This is in November.

Ms Bullock : The November statement.

Senator BRAGG: Then, when we go to the February statement, we go from 5.5 per cent growth in December 2025 down to negative 0.4 in June 2028. If I plot those two statement of monetary policy dwelling investment forecasts, the change between November last year and February this year looks quite pronounced to me. You're now projecting negative growth over the medium term—I assume you imagine that is the medium term.

Ms Bullock : I think our forecasts for dwelling investment reflect a view that it is difficult to get construction going in that area. I'm not familiar with the specifics of the forecasts. I'd have to take on notice exactly how we've come to those numbers.

Dr Kent : I think it's a feature of the updated forecasts, with an interest rate path that's higher under the assumptions.

Ms Bullock : That's part of it.

Dr Kent : Investment is a key transmission mechanism for monetary policy, so it is natural for dwelling investment growth to come down.

Senator BRAGG: The concern I have is that, if governments are focusing on housing and the Labor government here in Canberra is spending $45 billion on housing but we're getting negative growth projected, that's not good, is it?

Ms Bullock : It's not solving a supply problem. But, again, these are our forecasts based on what we think is going to happen based on a central projection of an interest rate rise.

Senator BRAGG: It's very concerning. Thank you. We'll look forward to your detailed answers on notice on that. Do you mind, Chair, if I continue to one other topic on housing?

CHAIR: You've got three more minutes.

Senator BRAGG: I'm always striving to be efficient and productive.

CHAIR: That's great. I appreciate that.

Senator BRAGG: I know that that's also how the bank feels about things. In terms of the five per cent deposit scheme, I get that you're not the lending regulator; that's APRA's role. But you do look at prudential risk in the system, don't you?

Ms Bullock : We look at macroprudential risks and financial stability risks broadly, not in terms of individual institutions.

Senator BRAGG: This is probably a very dumb question, but I know you have to field lots of dumb questions in your role, when you come to Canberra, so you're probably used to this! But do you have a loan-to-value ratio in your RBA policy book that is instructive about what a risky loan might be?

Ms Bullock : We don't have a 'policy book'.

Senator BRAGG: You know what I mean.

Ms Bullock : The usual rule of thumb is that anything over 80 is a bit risky. And there is some evidence that those loans at loan-to-valuation ratios over 80 are riskier than loans at lower loan-to-valuation ratios. But it all depends on the context. And this is risks to the banks, I should say; I'm talking about the potential impacts on the banks. At the moment, because of the rise in house prices, there's hardly anyone in negative equity. So risks to the banks, even at high loan-to-valuation ratios, are quite low because, if someone couldn't meet their repayments and, heaven forbid—awful situation—had to sell, they would not be selling at a loss, and they certainly wouldn't be selling at a rate that wouldn't give them the money needed to repay the bank. So, in terms of the risk to the financial institutions, even if it was over 80, it wouldn't necessarily be a massive risk to the institution at the moment. But 80 is the number, probably.

Senator BRAGG: But what about for the person? A 95 per cent loan is a risky loan, isn't it?

Senator O'NEILL: What's the default rate on those, though? Isn't that the indicator?

Senator BRAGG: I think you'll have your questions next. Do you want to ask me questions?

Senator O'NEILL: Well, you're constructing a fantasy here.

Senator BRAGG: Sorry, it's not a fantasy. Ninety-five per cent loans are a policy of your government.

Senator O'NEILL: You've had evidence here about the low default rate—

Senator HUME: Chair, could you intervene. Just allow Senator Bragg to finish his line of questioning.

CHAIR: Yes.

Senator BRAGG: Thanks, Senator Hume. I appreciate that, Deputy Chair. My question is: is a 95 per cent loan a risky loan?

Ms Bullock : It may or may not be. It all depends.

Senator BRAGG: Fair enough.

Ms Bullock : If it's a loan-to-valuation ratio of over 80 per cent, typically—not if you're a first home buyer now, but typically—you would have to get lenders mortgage insurance to address that. That's because the banks regard them as a riskier loan. The higher the loan-to-valuation ratio, then, yes, it's potentially riskier. But it depends in whose hands that loan is and it also depends on what I said is happening with the housing market, in case the risk to the banks might be different in different circumstances.

Senator BRAGG: But it is a bigger loan by definition, isn't it?

Ms Bullock : It's a bigger loan by definition.

Senator BRAGG: Yes.

Ms Bullock : If you are just taking as given the size of the loan, then, yes, it's riskier—potentially—if you borrow 95 per cent rather than 80 per cent.

Senator BRAGG: Basically, an interest rate rise would have a greater, disproportionate impact on someone with a 95 per cent loan.

Ms Bullock : Well, if you've borrowed more money, then you will be paying a higher interest rate on a larger loan, yes.

Senator BRAGG: Just finally, because I know others have questions—again, I understand your role may preclude you from answering this—when you look at the house prices at the entry level for younger people, do you think that they're too high?

Ms Bullock : Too high? That's a judgement. I wouldn't like to say they're too high, but it is harder for people. Ratios of housing prices to income now are higher than they've been in the past, so by definition it is harder for people to get in on the bottom rung of the ladder than it has been in the past, given an income.

Senator BRAGG: Thanks, Governor.

CHAIR: Senator Canavan.

Senator O'NEILL: That's why we have a five per cent deposit scheme—so they can get in.

Senator CANAVAN: I want to go to the Statement on monetary policy and, particularly, the table at the back of it—the real-wage price index. My reading of your forecast here is that, while there is some growth in real wages by the end of the forecast period, real wages will remain below where they are today through to mid-2028. Is that correct?

Ms Bullock : You've got to be a little bit careful just using the wage price index for that, because the wage price index doesn't actually measure what people are being paid. It doesn't include things like job changes, promotions, bonuses and those sorts of things. So, if you—

Senator CANAVAN: Let's just take the—

Ms Bullock : actually look at real wages—

Senator CANAVAN: It's the best measure we've got.

Ms Bullock : they are rising.

Senator CANAVAN: But, over that forecast period, they'll still be below, won't they?

Dr Kent : But I'm not sure it's the best measure we have.

Senator CANAVAN: What's the best measure you have?

Dr Kent : The national accounts measure is a much broader measure that picks up those—

Senator CANAVAN: You don't offer forecasts of that, then?

Ms Bullock : It picks up these things, and those numbers—I think they're still rising.

Dr Kent : That's what the nominal average earnings per hour are referring to.

Senator CANAVAN: But that's nominal, not real. Isn't it?

Dr Kent : Yes, but the wage price index is nominal as well. So you have to just—

Senator CANAVAN: Hang on. How can the real wage price index be nominal if it's called a real wage index?

Ms Bullock : No, no.

Dr Kent : No, the one here is the nominal wage price index growth.

Ms Bullock : On that table, under 'Income', is the wage price index. That's the nominal wage price index.

Senator CANAVAN: I'm getting confused. Is it real—is it after inflation?

Dr Kent : No.

Ms Bullock : No.

Senator CANAVAN: It's not? That's not a measure of real wages, then?

Ms Bullock : If you are looking—

Senator CANAVAN: I suppose, colloquially, when we say 'real wages'—

Ms Bullock : Oh, sorry. Sorry. No. He's looking at this one, Dr Kent.

Dr Kent : Oh, sorry. You're looking at—sorry.

Ms Bullock : The one you should be looking at is 'Real average earnings per hour', which is rising.

Senator CANAVAN: Which does start rising.

Ms Bullock : Which is rising.

Senator CANAVAN: But the real wage index actually—

Ms Bullock : Yes, but that doesn't, as I said, measure what people actually earn.

Senator CANAVAN: Has there been a period where—that index is now back to 2011 levels.

Dr Kent : Well, I think—

Senator CANAVAN: Can I just finish? You're very defensive on this point. Has there ever been a period in Australian economic history where we haven't had an increase in the real wage index for 17 years? In fact, it will still be quite a lot below.

Ms Bullock : I will have to take that on notice. We have graphs on the real wage—

Dr Kent : I'll try and find it.

Ms Bullock : We'll have to try and find it.

Senator CANAVAN: Real wages are back to 2011 levels today—they've gone back 15 years—and, Governor, you said before that the economy is 'okay'. I'm just trying to square your statement that the economy is okay with the feedback I get, as a representative of people, that people are really struggling. When you say the economy is okay, are you not taking into account how much people are struggling right now? Living standards have dropped like we've never seen before.

Ms Bullock : On the contrary, we do understand that not everyone is doing well. We do understand that.

Senator CANAVAN: I would put to you that it's not 'not everyone'; it's almost everyone who is not doing well.

Ms Bullock : Well, the economy—

Senator CANAVAN: When you've got that kind of drop—

Ms Bullock : If you go to—it's graph 2.7, which is 'Household disposable income growth'. What that shows you is that, over the past couple of years, real household disposable incomes have been rising.

Senator CANAVAN: Right. Are they—

Ms Bullock : That's what that tells you.

Senator CANAVAN: Are they back to levels they were before COVID?

Ms Bullock : If you look at the AENA measure of real income per hour worked, yes—

Senator CANAVAN: No, no.

Ms Bullock : they're well above.

Senator CANAVAN: This is part of the problem. You keep jumping around to different stats. I just asked: are real disposable incomes back to where they were before COVID?

Ms Bullock : Our preferred measure—yes, they're above.

Senator CANAVAN: Real disposable income?

Dr Kent : I believe it would be, but we'd have to take that on notice. Can I just make an important point here?

Senator CANAVAN: It seems to me that, whenever there's something that might be negative, you take it on notice, and then you try and jump to a different measure when you want to say something positive. I suppose people listening might be getting pretty frustrated, because, certainly, people don't feel like they're better off right now.

Dr Kent : But can I answer your question about these different measures?

Senator CANAVAN: Yes.

There have been 570,000 homes built since we came to government, 220 of those during the National Housing Accord period. Building approvals—that is, new homes coming into the market—have improved for three years in a row, with home starts up by 11 per cent on the same time last year. Construction costs, which are fundamental to getting the housing supply chain moving, have fallen from a half-century high under the coalition, with increases of 17.3 per cent down to below inflation at 1.8 per cent. It might look like a small change to people who have homes and comfortable incomes, but a 50 per cent increase in Commonwealth rent assistance is a very significant contribution indeed. That's what the government's plan is: it is a well-resourced, very significant allocation from the budget, unparalleled in our history. It's not perfect, but it is a big effort. It is unparalleled in our history and it's a very strong record of achievement. There are still challenges in the housing market; otherwise, you'd pull up stumps and not worry about it. I've also made some changes to the organisational structure. Currently, I have a chief investment officer who looks after our 'more homes', the social and affordable housing programs. I have two executive leaders that are responsible for the respective programs in homeownership. I have a CFO, a chief risk officer and a chief operating officer.

Senator BRAGG: What did the staff survey say? What was the key takeaway?

Mr Langford : The staff survey said, as a headline, that five out of 10 staff are very engaged—

Senator BRAGG: Five out of 10?

Mr Langford : 2½ are sitting in a neutral category and 2½ have expressed dissatisfaction.

Senator BRAGG: What do you think about that?

Mr Langford : When we look at the survey—and we take this very seriously—we understand. It's been a very challenging operating environment. There is a very contested policy space. There is frequent public commentary that many of our staff have taken very personally because they are putting in enormous efforts. We've also taken on board feedback that they've given us about clarity and communication. There is strong sentiment about the prolonged uncertainties through the course of last year in what was a very highly contested—it remains very highly contested—policy space; there was, in the election, a lot of uncertainty about Housing Australia's programs. That has created ongoing challenges for staff. We've had to build a lot of organisational systems and structures to cope with a much larger, expanded remit and the scale, risk and complexity of the organisation. There is really valuable feedback that staff have given us. We've given a number of briefings to staff and we've committed an action plan around the steps that we're taking to encourage a work environment where everyone feels they can come to work and do their best work and be well supported. I can step through the key themes of that if you'd like me to.

Senator BRAGG: So 50 per cent of the staff are not engaged?

Mr Langford : No, that's not what I said.

Senator BRAGG: Say it again, then.

Mr Langford : The survey tool we use tells us that five out of 10 staff—we had a very high response rate, in the order of 86 per cent.

Senator BRAGG: That's good.

Mr Langford : It's very positive that staff want to express their views. Senator BRAGG: So what are you going to do to drive the turnover rate down?

Senator BRAGG: So you've got some plans. The board discussed this, did they?

Senator BRAGG: I'm just trying to finish up with you because I know other people want to do stuff. Can you supply on notice a summary of the findings, the staff survey and whatever your rectification plan is, in broad terms, that went to the board and was discussed at the board on Tuesday.

Mr Langford : Yes. I would point out to you that there is a question on notice that we've already responded to, or it may be that it is yet to be tabled. We'll look at that in relation to the results, but I'm very happy to offer to take a question on notice in relation to the plan that we've got.

Senator BRAGG: Mr Rimmer, were you part of this discussion on Tuesday?
