Senator BARBARA POCOCK: I want to come back to a couple more issues. I'm really curious about the way in which HAFF projects get funded and where they get funded. It strikes me that these projects require considerable capacity in the applicant, and some places in Australia are better set up for that than others. They have more of a deeper history with community housing providers and so on, which leads me to think of this as a capacity based allocation as opposed to a needs based allocation. I think last time I mentioned Newcastle. I'm also thinking of places like the Riverland in my state or what we used to call the Iron Triangle. These are places with a lot of housing need with very limited capability. What do you say to the fact that HAFF needs to reach places with limited capability? What's its ability to really meet the need where it is?

Mr Rimmer : I might provide some answer to that but then ask Mr Langford to talk about the evaluation process that projects go through. HAFF is not the only program supporting social and affordable housing. For example, the Northern Territory remote housing program has a very specific target. It is what it says on the label. There are many state and territory programs that are suited to particular cohorts or particular geographic outcomes. Your characterisation of HAFF is, I think, accurate that it requires a degree of sophistication and capacity to engage directly with Housing Australia and the financial models that are involved in HAFF, but there's also the Social Housing Accelerator program that you've mentioned and a range of other programs. It's also the case that HAFF's outcomes from rounds 1 and 2 are pretty well distributed across jurisdictions.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: But the regions, I understand, really missed out.

Mr Rimmer : There is a reasonable distribution between metro and regional. Could it be better? Certainly. Are there improvements that are being made? That's actually why in HAFF round 3 there are four specific streams of funding now in place, one of which is—I'll get this name wrong—speciality and diversity.

Mr Langford : Housing diversity. Mr Rimmer, if you're happy, I'll pick up from there. I beg your pardon, Senator.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: No, go. I'm just thinking that I could get this probably on notice rather than hold up things here if it's—

Mr Langford : I could make a very brief remark, and then I'm happy to if you want further information. Certainly in round 3, as Mr Rimmer said, there are four funding streams. One of the mechanisms by which we are encouraging that capacity building that you're talking about, if I go to two specific streams, is working with states and territories. We can provide a commitment to a state or territory that allows them to bring together the project, and then they find the community housing provider that they want to work with. And we've encouraged them to think about areas that they could do that where they may be underserved and where the capacity of community housing providers may not be appropriate, and then they go through a process with us where effectively we and the state are working together to facilitate the outcome. That's been a big part of the construct of HAFF round 2, and it's something we've continued into HAFF round 3. It really starts from a recognition that, in particular in social housing, the states are the primary custodian of that system, and so supporting a range of outcomes, including in regions and with smaller providers, is an important way to do that.

I'd also add that the First Nations stream very specifically recognises that that is a nascent sector in many ways. There are some outstanding providers who do great work, but the establishment of the concierge service to work with applicants by Housing Australia is, in part, a recognition and response to how we support First Nations led housing organisations. It will have a different experience to it. And then, of course, there's the HAFF CT, quite separately—it's funding crisis and transitional accommodation—which does work with a lot more diverse providers.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: Thank you for that, and if there is any further information you want to give to me on notice, I'd appreciate the detail. Do you have any concerns about community housing provider 'cladding', if I can use that term, by profiteers, people, organisations or other financial sectors which clip the ticket at all levels of a project to make a nice tidy sum and then just make use, for the front of their application and their work, of a compliant community housing provider?

Mr Langford : This is an issue we thought deeply about very specifically in relation to round 3. It's something that we want to see a deeper evidence base for. Our experience in rounds 1 and 2 suggest that, by and large, these are very traditional community housing providers who are working with a range of partners, often in very established relationships. We've relied heavily on both the charities regulator and the community housing regulators for their checks and balances.

In round 3 there are additional tests that we're applying that are really going to deeper elements of control of that substance of the outcome. Much like in the First Nations stream, we are very focused on how we ensure very authentic outcomes in that stream and avoid 'cladding', to use your term, around an application. We want to ensure that it is appropriate for the private sector to play a role in the delivery of housing and the financing of it, because that is a way that we're mobilising additional resources and an ability to manage risk. But we also want to ensure that it is fairly renumerated, having regard to the risks that have been taken on, and so there are mechanisms of control that we have also used in rounds 1 and 2.

Without getting too technical, but effectively our agreement to provide our funding often comes with—think of it like a tripartite arrangement with funders and others. They are the most reasonable controls we have in place, and if you exceed returns of X then you may need to return money to the Commonwealth. We call it an intercreditor arrangement. They are really important mechanisms by which we are trying to ensure that value is being built, as Mr Rimmer referred to earlier, over time in the community housing sector so that HAFF is building a legacy that it will extend beyond the program.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: Thank you for that. Mr Rimmer, will you be undertaking a comparative analysis? You mentioned before that something like the accelerator does a different thing than the HAFF, and there are real maintenance costs and rental gap costs for social or low-income renters. It would be very interesting, would it not, to see an analysis of the first 5,000 homes and see how their costs compare to a direct funding of such housing through a community housing provider, building in rental subsidies, as necessary, and maintenance. It just seems to me we're doing a very complicated thing here, which is incredibly profitable for some people, without a long-term housing outcome in some cases. We could be doing it a different way, and Treasury, it seems to me, should be looking at the comparison.

Mr Rimmer : Part of our policy responsibility is accountability for social and affordable housing policy advice to ministers. As part of that, I have no doubt that we will do work of that kind in addition to our other evaluation processes that are set up, such as the legislated review.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: Thank you. My last set of questions go to the question of the revolving door and the role of advisers. As reported in the media, one of the housing minister's policy advisers has recently made the move to the Commonwealth Bank—one of the big four banks that is certainly making a lot of money out of bigger home loans partly driven by the changes to the five per cent deposit scheme. This is the same bank that just yesterday announced that enormous profit of over $5 billion. When will that officer begin that new role?

Senator Ayres: Senator Pocock, I appreciate you haven't used the staffer's name.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: I'm not using the name.

Senator Ayres: I appreciate that.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: I'm interested in some principles here, but I'd like to know when they are starting.

Senator Ayres: Let me answer the question to the extent that I can. I have noticed in one other incident around this place that somebody decided it was okay to do that, to name a person who can't defend themselves.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: It's on the public record.

Senator Ayres: It wasn't you, but somebody did. And, as a matter of deep regret, I hope they've reflected upon that. I'll just use this opportunity to make that point because, in my view, it was pretty bad form and not the way that these questions are usually approached. What I can tell you—and I'll come back to you on notice, if that's required, to provide anything else we can provide—is that person is not working in a role that has anything to do with housing.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: In their new role?

Senator Ayres: In their new role, yes.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: My question is: when do they start?

Senator Ayres: I understand that that's your question. It's just that that's what I know. If there's anything else we can provide you, we will.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: So you will provide me with when they start?

Senator Ayres: If we can, yes.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: What obligations or requirements does such a person have as they move to an institution which will find much of their special knowledge of interest?

Senator Ayres: I think I've answered that in my previous answer—that is, I don't believe, on the basis of what I know about this, that that person is working in an area that has anything to do with the responsibilities that they discharged on behalf of the minister or the work that they were doing.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: Minister, the Lobbying Code of Conduct says that a person who was previously employed in the office of a minister:

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: You don't see them as being required to meet any obligation in relation to—

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: They're not engaged in any lobbying, but the definition of 'lobbying' is influencing decision-making. There would be an influential person in there.

That is not the function they are performing.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: Do you have concerns, Minister, about the rotation of people from key influential roles in your government into very profitable institutions where their knowledge would be of great interest to senior decision-makers?

Senator Ayres: There is a ministerial staff code of conduct. It has been followed scrupulously. That gives me confidence, and it should give others confidence, that the right thing has happened here. The code of conduct is designed to deal with the kinds of apprehensions that you might have about these kinds of issues, and it's being followed.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: I certainly do have those concerns. I think there is a great deal of evidence that the revolving door is incredibly profitable for large organisations.

Senator Ayres: Not in this case.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: So I look forward to any information you can give me on that outside of this, and I'm very happy to take it privately. Thank you.

CHAIR: Senator Canavan.

Senator CANAVAN: I want to ask a housing question, particularly on international developments. It seems that Canada and New Zealand to a certain extent are seeing some moderation, even some decreases, in their housing costs. Both countries seem to have taken a fairly aggressive stance on migration and reduced those levels. Have you looked at the relationship between migration and housing prices around the world and whether or not the approach of Canada and New Zealand is working?

Mr Rimmer : No.

Senator CANAVAN: Where are you from, Treasury or housing?

Mr Rimmer : Treasury; the Treasury's housing group.

Senator CANAVAN: Why haven't you done that? Why haven't you looked at what might work overseas?

Mr Rimmer : We're continuously looking for overseas experience about housing policy. We're also working closely with colleagues across government, including colleagues responsible for migration policy in the Department of Home Affairs. But you asked a very specific question, and the answer to your very specific question was no.

Senator CANAVAN: It's had a lot of reporting. The Canadian experience, in particular, is having a lot of focus and attention right now. We've got this massive housing issue, and we've had a massive surge in immigration alongside it. It's just strange that you haven't looked at it. Have you made any attempt to analyse the effects of the unprecedented level of migration we've seen in the last few years and the housing market outcomes for young Australians in particular?

Mr Rimmer : We look at the relationship between migration and housing demand. The National Housing Supply and Affordability Council looks at that on a routine basis in their annual report. It's a complicated relationship for all kinds of reasons, including that skilled migrants can add to our capacity to meet housing supply challenges. Beyond that—

Senator CANAVAN: No doubt that's all true, but you've got it as a real-world example now. In theory, there are always lots of different effects. You've got a real-world situation going on overseas. We have people marching on our streets against migration levels; two-thirds of Australians want migration to come down. I just don't understand why you're not even asking the question and not able to give us answers on this issue that is obviously of keen concern to Australians.

Mr Rimmer : We're not responsible for migration policy.

Senator CANAVAN: No, but you are responsible for housing policy.

Mr Rimmer : Sure, and we provide policy advice—

Senator CANAVAN: You can't even tell me whether our high levels of migration have made housing outcomes for Australians worse.

Senator Ayres: Reluctant as I am to reflect upon the market conditions in Canada, given the last couple of weeks, the truth is that a range of factors impact house prices in Canada. Recent data shows zero per cent growth in their economy—zero per cent growth, a stagnant economy.

Senator CANAVAN: We've got zero per cent real per capita growth. We've got negative, actually.

Senator Ayres: It's true that a stagnant economy does often—not always, but often—lead to falling prices of assets, including homes. That's true. We're roughly growing one-and-a-bit per cent to just a bit over two per cent on average, year on year.

Senator CANAVAN: Not in per capita terms.

Senator Ayres: That is a different outcome. I'm for economic growth. I'm for rising wages. I'm for more employment. I'm for a bigger economy. I'm for more economic resilience.

Senator CANAVAN: My question, though, is: why isn't the government looking at this issue? You can do a Google search and tell me a few stats, but my question is why the government hasn't asked for detailed advice on whether the rate of migration we've been experiencing is exacerbating the situation for Australians—especially, as I say, young Australians—who just want to own their own home.

Senator Ayres: The government considers all sorts of factors. I take exception to the Google search observation.

Senator CANAVAN: Was it AI? Was it ChatGPT?

Senator Ayres: Somebody else did it for me.

Mr Rimmer : You're giving him too much credit!

Senator Ayres: You're giving me far too much credit here. But a range of factors—

Senator CANAVAN: But why haven't you asked?

Senator Ayres: The government looks at all of these questions across all of the economic settings. I know that there's a school of thought—we'll see what happens over the next couple of days. There's a section of the Liberal and National parties that is all about importing extremist ideas and exporting jobs; I understand that. Whether that's the sort of grouping that has more sway or not, we'll see.

Senator CANAVAN: I think I deserve a response to that. As I say, it's very clear in every poll that's asked that two-thirds of Australians want migration levels to come down.

Senator Ayres: The government has taken a very responsible approach to migration.

Senator CANAVAN: The idea that you would label two-thirds of Australians as having 'extreme views' is unbelievable.

Senator Ayres: That's not what I said. I said you lot are the extremists.

Senator CANAVAN: We're representing the two-thirds of Australians who want migration to come down.

CHAIR: One person talking at a time.

Senator Ayres: That's why you keep getting smaller: more and more imported extremist ideas.

Senator CANAVAN: Not only are you not listening to those people, but you're not even asking the question about whether what they are concerned about is real.

Senator Ayres: And you wonder why the centre of Australians don't want anything to do with you.

CHAIR: Senator Canavan, do you have any more questions?

Senator CANAVAN: No, that'll do me.

Throughout his career, Dr Warrington has led significant pieces of work, including using the National Measurement Institute's expertise to respond to COVID-19 and provide advice to reform and streamline Australia's measurement law. I wish Dr Warrington and his family all the very best in the future and thank him for his excellent career.

Senator Ayres: Bruce has played an extraordinary leadership role in a piece of scientific and metrological infrastructure that is so important for Australia—in economic terms, in science and research terms and in terms of our electricity and energy systems. He's come through as a technical person into a CEO role, and quite a challenging role in terms of where the assets of that are up to. He's well loved by his staff. Every time I go there, I see the extraordinary relationship he has with his staff. I want to pass on my congratulations to him at this point, as well.

Senator CANAVAN: Yes, I got that. I'm also very much aware that Glencore is a very savvy business, and good luck to them. Senator CANAVAN: When you say 'assessment' or 'review points', is that defined in the agreement towards particular financial metrics, or is it simply that there'll be an assessment at the time and the details of that are left up to when it's done?

Ms Talbot : There are a range of details in the contract, but I'm not at liberty to reveal those. They are commercial in confidence. The contract with the company is—

Senator CANAVAN: I'm not asking for the particular thresholds.

Ms Quinn : There are specific arrangements—

Ms Quinn : There are specific negotiated measures which are clear to all parties about what the terms of the review points are, particularly for the first two years. Senator Ayres: Broadly, there's a history here in Mount Isa. Senator CANAVAN: I'll just ask this question and I might come back to it because this is a little bit detailed. I've got the federal financial agreement now. There is milestone 1, 30 April 2026. I'm struggling to see which of those conditions actually relate to the profitability of Glencore's operations. That's my question, but maybe we can come back to it because we're at 10 minutes.

Ms Quinn : My team will correct me, but I think it correlates with the first item.

Ms Quinn : The team will correct me—I haven't got it in front of me, unfortunately, but the team might—but it's the very first item.

Senator CANAVAN: So the financial assistance agreement is something we don't have?

Ms Quinn : Yes, and it's captured in there. They have to conform to that, which, broadly speaking, is related to their financial viability.

CHAIR: Thank you. Senator McDonald?

Senator McDONALD: Well, this is tidy, because my questions follow up on the same topic. Does the bailout package include the capital cost for the rebricking of the smelter this year, in 2026?

Ms Quinn : It does have capital components related to the operation of the business, yes.

Senator McDONALD: Okay, so, if Glencore were to come back and say that they're going to ask for money for rebricking this year, you would be surprised?

Senator McDONALD: There was a media release, I think it was today, 'Mount Isa transformation study to shape region's next chapter', and it talked about expressions of interest. Senator Ayres: We'll all be part of it. There's a shared approach to that. Glencore will play its part in that work. Senator McDONALD: Given that Glencore owns the lease that the smelter is on, how do you see it will work? That there will be a proper examination of new technology, alternate sites, possibly a buy or acquisition of the site should Glencore decide that they know longer want it—I'm spitballing here. What role will there be for that input if Glencore has obviously got a vested interest in what those opinions might be?

Senator Ayres: What the release really does is say we're going to identify somebody to run that process. Of course, everybody who's engaged in that, at a commercial level, has different interests. I don't want to spitball, as you say, Senator McDonald, about the potential views that people might bring to that process. But it is a region that's rich in mineral resources where there are, in some places, junior miners who have really made a go of resources that other operations have struggled with. There's room for optimism, but it won't happen by itself. And so that facilitation is designed to get a hold of what the medium- and long-term issues are that the two governments and the industrial and resources players in the region need to commit to addressing.

Senator McDONALD: You've drawn my attention to something that I'd perhaps, very optimistically, incorrectly filled in some gaps on. This media release is calling for an expression of interest to be the proponent to carry out the transformation study. I had, in my enthusiasm, read it as expressions of interest to make submissions to the study.

Senator Ayres: No. I'll let the department talk to the timetable for that. This is moving fast to get a process up and about. I'll get the officials to go to the completion date of the transformation study, but it's certainly not an endless process.

Ms Quinn : Yes, at a high level, there's all the proponents to the agreement—Queensland government, Commonwealth government and Glencore. They are parties to the transformation study. Senator McDONALD: Sorry, just to clarify that—it will be for company XYZ to draw in the submissions to write the technical paper and to—

Ms Quinn : And to work with the Commonwealth, Glencore, the Queensland government and others—

Senator McDONALD: Yes, and others.

Ms Quinn : to look at the opportunities in the region. It is the analytical support for the process, but there is a governance to the process. It's asking for people to help in the process, but it's not the whole element of it.

Senator McDONALD: And that's funded from the $200 million for the first year. Can I ask how much is going towards the transformation study?

Ms Quinn : That is commercial in confidence. Particularly, if we've put out an expression of interest, there are commercial discussions in terms of paying for it.

Senator McDONALD: Okay. But you'll be giving some guidance to whoever is making the application, whether it's 50c or $50 million.

Ms Quinn : Sure.

Senator McDONALD: I'm still struggling to understand a little bit that if Glencore's a party to the transformation study, and then the study starts throwing out things that are not in Glencore's perceived best interest, will you have a process that the national interest comes first, and that they don't get to rule in or rule out studies or ideas that they may not want to see?

Ms Talbot : If I may, that's correct. The study's purpose is to provide a comprehensive assessment of the economic potential of the whole region of the North West Minerals Province in Queensland. It is much broader than just Glencore. The expression of interest, just to clarify, has been put out by the Queensland government for somebody to undertake the transformation study and that does include a range of scope and terms of reference of the things that will be covered in the study, which are much broader than just the copper smelter itself.

Senator McDONALD: Will Glencore make a financial contribution to that study, given that at the moment they're in receipt of funds from the state and the Commonwealth?

Ms Talbot : The transformation study will be funded out of that first year of funding that you've identified.

Senator McDONALD: So they're not making a contribution per se. They are the happy recipients of that study being done. That's a characterisation. That's fine. Just back to the study: we've identified that it's going to be an external contractor doing that work.

Ms Talbot : Not entirely. Just to be clear, the Commonwealth will bring its capabilities. The state will bring its capabilities. We'll be drawing on other areas—people, contribution. But clearly you need someone to kind of orchestrate and help combine.

Senator McDONALD: Yes.

Ms Talbot : A secretariat service, almost. But we will be providing analysis from the department into that process as well, and we would expect the Queensland government to do so in terms of the information it holds on opportunities in the area. So it's not going to be sent off to do some analytical research in the corner. It's going to be a live, dynamic process.

Senator McDONALD: No.

Ms Talbot : You've raised some issues about conflicts. Different proponents are going to have different views about what they want to happen in the region. The view is that there's a need to have a proper, rigorous process about what the options are to look at the different scenarios. So it's unlikely that it's going to say, 'This is the one true solution.' It's going to be much more of a scenario analysis.

Senator McDONALD: Yes. As to this external contractor or whoever's the successful proponent for providing the secretariat for the study, I'm very keen that there be some of that expertise, as you say, which isn't housed in government departments; it's housed in the brightest of industrial minds.

Senator Ayres: I've discovered that there are a lot of people who've had a lot of experience in that facility and around it and who've got strong views and expertise.

Senator McDONALD: It's not a slight, but it's just not normally governments that come up with the best solutions.

Senator Ayres: No, I'm just saying there is expertise around. There are all sorts of people engaged in this process who've got an iron in the fire in terms of some of these things—people who are engaged in it because they actually just deeply care about the region.

Senator McDONALD: I'll just finish up on this point.

Senator Ayres: We want to bring as much of that together as possible.

Senator McDONALD: For example, the Port of Townsville has just built a new temporary hard load stand. The rail operators are bringing on additional resources to support not Glencore but other miners in the region. So I think there's a lot of interest in making sure we get this right. I'll come back in my next round. Thank you.

CHAIR: Senator Canavan.

Senator COLBECK: We keep moving up and down the table! I'll just go back to the Industry Growth Program. I've got a couple of quick questions to follow on with that. Ms Oliver : That's right. We have some colleagues joining us at the table who are leading on Liberty Bell Bay.

Senator COLBECK: Has the government received a specific request for assistance from the Tasmanian government, from the Premier?

Mr Sloan : We are in constant conversation with our Tasmanian colleagues, and I don't think it would be appropriate to disclose those confidential conversations.

Senator Ayres: I'll let the official continue on the detail, but I might just make a couple of comments about this.

Senator COLBECK: Can I say that, before you do, I understand the difficulties around the company. We're on the same page on that side of things.

This company recently—some years ago but in recent history—was well capitalised and was efficiently producing exports, including to the United States, and had certainty of supply chain in terms of the product it received. We are obviously keeping a very close eye on it and, at my level, have been engaged with the Tasmanian government. At the official level, that engagement has been constant. I have watched the efforts that the Tasmanian government has made, including recently extraordinary steps to—

Senator COLBECK: I'll note your comments with respect to the fact that it was running well, running viably, and had solid supply chains with supply of material and delivery of material into its export markets. It is an important employer in that neck of the woods—

Senator COLBECK: And the fact that the workforce is still there is important—and the fact that, as you've indicated, they're still paid. It's important not just for the business itself but also for its tentacles out into that northern community—

The department officials are very diligent in terms of the way that we've worked through the assessments and the engagement with the Tasmanian government. Senator COLBECK: I'll walk around the corner from Liberty Bell Bay to Bell Bay Aluminium. This is, I think, a bit of a weird one really. The reason that Bell Bay Aluminium is in Tassie, where it is, is because it's had access to a reliable source of energy from Hydro Tas for a long time at very competitive rates. I think it's something of the order of 20 per cent of the Tasmanian grid, so it's an important player in that context as well. It seems to me very perverse that a company that is producing aluminium using green energy, that has reduced its CO2 emissions over the last 30 years by probably 50 per cent—because reducing energy utilisation is an efficiency that it gains because aluminium is basically solid energy pretty much—and yet it faces genuine difficulty in accessing the scheme that's set up to support green aluminium production because of its legacy. I just find that really perverse that you potentially lose one of the cleanest producers of aluminium globally in terms of its CO2 outputs, but it's facing exactly the same pressures as everybody else. How do we make that not happen?

Senator Ayres: I'll just make a couple of headline comments about that and then go to officials on it. Really, there's a limited amount I can say because of the status of the—

Senator Ayres: The green aluminium production credit is still under design, so there's a limited amount that I can say about that. That's the first thing. The second thing is there are smelters that are sourcing lower cost renewable energy contracts, and we're working through that process. The third thing is—you're absolutely right—that facility is there in Tasmania because it's had access to low-cost hydro power from publicly owned Hydro Tasmania. Senator COLBECK: On my final point—having been wound up by the chair—I know that Minister Duigan, the Tasmanian minister, has said his view is that it should qualify for the production credit scheme. You've said that that program is still under design. I will add my advocacy to that of Minister Duigan and the Premier in respect of that scheme because, as I said before, I can't see how you could lose a facility that's producing, competitively, green aluminium for other sites that might still be using other energy sources.

Senator Ayres: I don't know if there's anything officials want to add, but I—

Senator COLBECK: I accept I'm making a comment. I get that, Minister, but I'm delivering my message to add to Minister Duigan's. Thank you, Chair.

CHAIR: Senator Hodgins-May.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: I've got some questions about major project status. Can I confirm that this is the right part of the program.

Ms Quinn : It is.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: Thank you. On 3 July 2025, Minister Ayres announced the major project status of Bonaparte CCS in a media release in which it was labelled a 'large-scale renewable energy' venture. Did the department provide advice to the minister or his office on how Bonaparte, a CCS project, can be labelled as a renewable energy project in the context of this announcement?

Ms Quinn : While I wait for officials to join, at a very high level the Major Projects Facilitation Agency does assess proponents against set criteria as to whether they meet the required status to be passed through to the minister for decision. We do provide advice against the criteria, but it is the minister's decision at the end. We would have looked at the criteria as identified, but, as to the specifics of your question, I'll pass to my colleague.

Ms Gannon : I'm sorry, Senator, but could you repeat that last bit of the question?

Senator HODGINS-MAY: Did the department provide advice to the minister on how Bonaparte, a CCS project, can be labelled as a renewable energy project in the context of the announcement?

Ms Gannon : As to the specifics of your question, Senator, I'd have to take that on notice and go back to what advice was provided at the time. But, as the secretary said, the criteria against which we provide advice to the minister on whether a project should or shouldn't be designated as a major project and have major project status are set out on the department's website. It looks at the strategic significance of the investment, whether it faces complex regulatory challenges and the financial viability of the project.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: Is it possible to table the advice that you would have provided as well?

Ms Gannon : Again, I'll look into that. One of the barriers we have to providing that advice is that it contains typically a great deal of commercially sensitive information, and the other is that, through the course of the advice, it demonstrates our methodology in assessing the applications that we receive. We're reluctant to release information that might allow future proponents to anticipate our methodology and game it. But I can look into that for you.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: I'm probably less interested in the methodology, but anything that speaks to it as being a renewable energy project—

Ms Gannon : Of course.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: I suppose that follows into my next question. Is 'large-scale renewable energy venture' a formal category under major project status, or was that just the communication used for that particular one?

Ms Quinn : There's not a split between different activities. The list of activities of projects that have been identified as major projects covers the Renewable Energy Hub, the nickel project, the hydrogen project and various other things. The broad criteria were as my colleague outlined, which relate to it being a significant project, the regulatory complexity and the like. It's not targeted at specific areas of the economy.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: So that's not a specific bucket. Do you know who would have given it that label as a large-scale renewable energy project? Who would that have been?

Ms Quinn : In all likelihood, it was the characterisation of the project we would take from the company itself, because it is the one which understands what its project is, but it would have been backed up by the material that it provided to verify what it is that they're undertaking.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: If there is any more information about that that can be provided—whether it did actually come from the company, the comms department or somewhere else—I'd be grateful for that.

Ms Quinn : I'm happy to look into it.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: In January of this year, Inpex announced it had withdrawn Bonaparte's CCS project from environmental assessment. Does this change or alter its major project status?

Ms Gannon : No. With those regulatory processes that the companies are working through, we provide support as they navigate them, but I'm not aware of anything that's happened that's resulted in that status being withdrawn.

Ms Quinn : The process of the major projects authority is to go back and look at projects over time, and some projects have lost their status as a result of how long they've been in the program and how far they have gone through the steps, because we do try and focus our resources on those that are more prospective. There are review points. I'm not sure whether the timing has worked out such that anything that's happened in the project has hit a review point yet.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: Inpex has signalled it will resubmit its environmental assessment once changes to the regulations of the EPBC Act come into place. Does DISR have an understanding, or have you sought advice from DCCEEW colleagues or maybe even from Inpex itself, about what changes it is waiting for?

Ms Quinn : This is a matter that we are working with our department of environment colleagues on, because there were some changes in the EPBC Act legislation that went through the House that have implications for the way aspects of the offshore regulation for gas projects work, and we are working through that. My resource colleagues will be here a bit later, and they can provide more information on it. At a high level, the regulation changes mean that we need to change some of the offshore regulation, which will affect the way NOPSEMA deal with various aspects of their environmental approvals.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: Could you please table any correspondence between Inpex and DISR regarding its major project status approval last year.

Ms Quinn : We'll take it on notice, noting the caveats that my colleague talked about regarding commercial-in-confidence and the like.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: Does it flow to say that Inpex will automatically retain major project status upon resubmission of its environmental assessment?

Ms Quinn : It depends on whether they meet our criteria when we review the process. It's not linked in such a direct way. The Major Projects Facilitation Agency reviews the projects in a steady and sensible way. At that time, there'll be an assessment of what assistance it needs, what the likelihood of the project is and whether it continues to meet the criteria for major project status.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: You don't have any further information you can provide now about why it withdrew something that was touted as a large-scale renewable venture.

Ms Quinn : Other than what you've stated—which is that it's waiting for regulatory clarification post legislative change, which seems eminently sensible because there are links between the offshore gas regulatory environment and the environmental regulations, and we need to make sure that they work together. That is work that the government is working through. There are other proponents who are also waiting for clarity on how those obligations will be met under the new regulatory regime.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: Does the department know what percentage of storage at Bonaparte is proposed to be CO2 from hard-to-abate industries like metal and chemical refining, as touted by the government, versus CO2 from fossil fuel production?

Ms Quinn : I think we actually had question on this last time—I'm reading the Hansard. I'm not sure if that was part of their application for major project status. We can check.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: Last time, I think, I was directed to this part of the program to ask this question.

Ms Quinn : So the question is was it part of their application for major project status. That level of detail may not have been—

Senator HODGINS-MAY: What percentage is proposed to be from CO2 from hard-to-abate industries like metal and chemical refining versus CO2 from fossil fuel production?

Ms Gannon : We had a question on notice that went to this question, from the last estimates. We understand the project will initially focus on the storage of CO2 for Inpex's own projects, with the potential to seek sequester CO2 from third parties. That's the extent of the information I have from that question.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: So it's just CO2 from their own project?

Ms Quinn : Yes, which is predominantly related to gas extraction.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: Would you still, then, if that is the case, consider this a renewable energy project?

Ms Quinn : I'm not sure that's something we've assessed anything against.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: But it was labelled as a large-scale renewable energy venture in an announcement by the minister in July of last year.

Senator Ayres: It was a long time ago. I don't know about the labels that were attached to the project. I would just make the point that gas, particularly in the context that I work in, in terms of its industrial use, is a very important feature of our industrial energy mix. There are opportunities, particularly in areas where coal is currently being utilised, to lower emissions profiles very significantly by using gas. There are some obstacles to that because it's a very expensive. It seems—

Senator HODGINS-MAY: But surely you can't describe it as a large-scale renewable energy project. That seems a bit of a stretch.

It assumes that there will be further policy action that occurs between now and 2050 to bring about that end. That's the nature of the net zero projections. The forecasts that we do within the Resources and energy quarterly are done much more on a commercial basis and much more short-term forecast, so there is a gap in methodology across those two.

Senator McDONALD: I guess that makes sense to me, because I couldn't quite align roughly 30 per cent of Australia's export earnings coming from coal and gas and iron ore, yet the net zero transformational modelling seemed to say that we would be out of exports and out of money pretty rapidly. Ms Quinn : For different purposes.

Senator McDONALD: For reality, is where we're going, isn't it? What are the different purposes for resources, then?

Ms Ossolinski : No, not for resources, in the sense that the activities are undertaken for different purposes. The work that the department does, to look at the outlook for resources over the near term, is to provide information to the market to proponents in the system. It also feeds into considerations in other parts of the department. The exercise that the Treasury undertook for the net zero exercise was a particular modelling exercise, which they have articulated in public, which was around supporting government decision-making on net zero decisions, and they are different horizons, different activities.

Senator McDONALD: Activities at cross-purposes, I would have thought, the resources the department is trying to, I believe, facilitate, additional and successful mining activity for Australians and Australian investors. And the tax department one—I'm not quite sure where it was used, because it wasn't reflected in revenue group. It just seemed to be a standalone document.

Ms Quinn : As a department of state, we support the government in their policy objectives, which is to reduce emissions in Australia over time. The government policy, and we supported the government to develop this, was the net zero reduction plan for the resources sector. We certainly work towards policy aims of the government.

The purpose of the Resources and energy quarterly outlook is to do near-term forecasting of export volumes and prices. They're different elements. One is a near-term forecast. The other one is policy development and scenarios in order to inform government decision-making. They obviously can link, but they have very different purposes.

Senator McDONALD: What sorts of policy changes would your department be working on to assist the government's goal of reducing fossil fuel exports?

Ms Quinn : They're outlined in the resources, the net zero resources plan and the Future Gas Strategy. There are elements in there to do with carbon capture and storage, to do with reducing emissions from fugitive gases. I'll hand to my colleague to go through the other items.

Mr Jeremenko : Yes, reducing venting and flaring of gas projects. There is a considerable amount that was outlined in that Resources Sector Plan, which I can pull up some further detail on if you're interested, Senator.

Senator BARBARA POCOCK: Well, I am interested. I think that the highlight of the Future Gas Strategy was the overall concept of reducing supply down to a projected reduced demand. Senator BARBARA POCOCK: I'm sorry. I just missed what you first said.

Ms Ossolinski : Sorry. I can say that the Treasury did indeed use the IEA's trajectories for demand for various commodities and for the outlook, and I can comment on those trajectories if you are interested.

CHAIR: Senator Hodgins-May.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: I have some questions on the Gas Market Review, and I'm taking up the minister on his offer to discuss that in this part of the program. My questions relate to the rumoured bulk buy of gas to support industrial facilities as a possible outcome or solution, either as part of the Gas Market Review or in parallel to the gas reserve being considered. Can the department please explain how a—maybe hypothetical for now—bulk buy would operate and confirm whether this would involve government purchasing gas and onselling it to companies at below market rates.

Ms Quinn : There are quite a few hypotheticals in that. In general, in other circumstances where the government does bulk-purchase activities—for example, the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme—and other elements, it uses scale and aggregated demand to be able to negotiate in a market that may not be a balanced market in terms of competitive dynamics. So, in theory, there's a possibility that aggregating up demand might be able to result in a better commercial outcome, and that could be then shared with the individual customers that have been aggregated. That's the theory in terms of if there's an imbalance between supply and demand or imbalance between the number of suppliers and the number of demanders. There would be a whole set of policy considerations you'd need to do in that framework along the lines of how you would aggregate, how you would distribute and how you would do that sort of work. But that's the basic theory. If there's an imbalance between many different purchasers and a smaller number of sellers then you can reshape the market through aggregation.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: Have you provided any formal advice on that to government yet?

Ms Quinn : I don't believe so. It comes up; some stakeholders have suggested it. We would provide information in terms of what's in the market, what people are asking for and what they're discussing. In that sense, we probably have provided some form of advice to ministers.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: When you say 'stakeholders', that means government ministers?

Ms Quinn : No. There are proponents in the market, industrial users, who feel like they don't have enough market information. The whole consultation for the Gas Market Review was around asymmetric information between purchasers and sellers of gas and the ability to negotiate appropriate contracts that match the needs of industrial facilities. There have been ongoing public and private discussions around the prices that people are able to negotiate. In those discussions, the question has come up of what the different policy options available to the government are. The government, in response to the Gas Market Review, announced the further investigation of a reservation scheme for gas, and we are certainly working on that policy. That's the priority for the work we're doing in response to the Gas Market Review, along with other changes to the gas market to improve long-term contracting and transparency of prices.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: Do you think that that bulk buy could be characterised as a subsidy?

Ms Quinn : It depends on how it's characterised. Often, a rebalancing of the market conditions isn't itself necessarily a subsidy; it could be characterised as a correction of a market failure, depending on the underlying dynamics of the market. A subsidy really is a sort of theoretical proposition, in the sense of what price would be achieved in an efficient and effective market and whether that would be different from what would happen if the government intervened. It is the case that government can intervene in markets to result in an efficient and effective outcome, and that's usually not characterised as a subsidy.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: Out of curiosity—and maybe this is for the minister—why was reducing our carbon emissions or phasing out gas not a term of reference in the Gas Market Review?

Senator Ayres: Sorry, I didn't catch the first half of the question.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: Why wasn't reducing our carbon emissions or phasing out gas part of the terms of reference of the Gas Market Review?

Senator Ayres: The objectives of the review were as they were set out; that is, making sure that we have sufficient Australian gas for Australian users and that our gas reserves are used to deliver more investment in Australian industry. There are, in some sectors, very significant emissions reduction opportunities—for example, from moving from coal to gas. On the government's broader approach on the industrial side—we're in resources, but just allow me to move back across to my favourite subject—there is, for example, the Net Zero Fund, the $5 billion concessional at the bond rate minus one as the target rate; it is designed to support Australian businesses and industrial firms, particularly where, for example, gas is used as a heat source, to be able to access new capital to make them more efficient and able to use electricity or thermal batteries or whatever the technology is that suits their production processes. There will always be, subject to technological developments, some sections of Australian industry where gas is either very hard to eliminate or, as we've discussed before, a part of the chemical process of producing a product as a feedstock.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: Yes, I do understand the complexities—

Senator Ayres: So all those things—

Senator HODGINS-MAY: of the hard-to-abate industries. I suppose—

Ms Quinn : I've just looked at the gas market terms of reference, and the review was asked to examine the effectiveness and coherence of specific mechanisms identified, including the Australian Domestic Gas Security Mechanism, the heads of agreement and the domestic code of conduct, et cetera, in the context of ensuring that it achieves the government's objectives and the principles of the Future Gas Strategy, including supporting decarbonisation of the Australian economy—

Senator HODGINS-MAY: Is that the preamble or the terms of reference?

Ms Quinn : It was being very clear that the specific focus of the review was on the specific elements in achieving the overall government objectives. So I don't think the characterisation—it's not that the government's overall decarbonisation objectives were not included in the terms of reference. They definitely were in the terms of reference—

Senator HODGINS-MAY: But they're not one of the A to H terms of reference—

Ms Quinn : No, because they were very specific things that all needed to be considered in the context of achieving the government's decarbonisation objectives and the principles of the Future Gas Strategy, which was clearly to achieve net zero by 2050. The way I would characterise it is that there was a narrower—looking at the regulatory architecture that would deliver within the commitment to achieve net zero.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: I don't see how new gas achieves decarbonisation, but thanks for the clarification. It's been a few days since I've asked this and I think I was directed to ask it here as well—or maybe I wasn't asked, but I'm choosing to! Is a tax on gas exports on the table?

Ms Quinn : That is a matter for the Australian Treasury, who look at taxation policy.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: And do you consult with them on these sorts of proposals? Does the minister?

Ms Quinn : Well, yes. We talk to each other about anything, but they own the tax regulatory policy regime, particularly—

Senator HODGINS-MAY: Yes. I understand that. Have you provided advice to them on this particular policy?

Ms Quinn : As I understand it, the last time we had detailed conversations around the reforms to the PRRT, the petroleum resource rent tax, which was some years ago, there was detailed analysis and work jointly in that and there would be some follow-ups on those sorts of things. That was the last time there was significant engagement between the two departments.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: When was that, sorry?

Ms Quinn : I'd have to check, but I think it was about three years ago, from my recollection, but I'm happy to take it on notice. It was the changes to the PRRT that were announced by the Treasurer in a budget at some stage.

Mr Jeremenko : That's right. I think it was 2023. But we can correct that on notice if I'm wrong.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: Yes. Thank you. This may be for the minister: I'm really keen to get, and I think many Australians are keen to get, a firm understanding of whether this proposal is being taken seriously, considering the epic rip-off of these gas exports pumping up our domestic prices and paying minimal export tax. Even if we have a gas reservation policy, it just means companies meet their supply obligations and then continue to ship the majority of gas overseas while the broken petroleum resource rent tax provides basically zero compensation to everyday Australians. The fact that this hasn't been examined in four years, when it is most certainly in the public interest to be exploring this, warrants some reflection.

Senator Ayres: The intervention that Minister Bowen and I were unable to announce with the resources minister was an announcement of hers. That there was a decision to deliver a reservation strategy is a very substantial intervention into the Australian gas market. It's been talked about for 25 years but never delivered. We've had a gas market that is not operated in the interests of Australians. It is a very significant intervention. In terms of taxation matters, I don't want to direct you back in time to the Treasury crowd, but I'm sure they'd be delighted to answer your questions about these matters. The industry paid $11.8 billion in tax receipts during 2023-24. That's not nothing. So they meet their obligations there. I understand the argument that is made around the place, but the government's focus at the moment is the most significant intervention in a generation into this market.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: On a related but slightly different topic, the acreage that's just been released for exploration expressions of interest in the Otway Basin in my home state of Victoria—is this in direct response to the supposed need to find supply for Australia's east coast?

Ms Quinn : It's certainly consistent with the Future Gas Strategy, which had an element to ensure that future acreages were near other acreage releases and took into account the information that's available to the market. So it's very consistent with the direction set out in the Future Gas Strategy. It is the case that there are forecast gaps in supply for the east coast market, and there will be a need for an expansion of supply to meet expected demand. It's part of the overall Future Gas Strategy, which was to release acreages in an efficient and effective way. I'll just pass to my colleague, if he'd like to add anything.

Mr Jeremenko : The only thing I'd add is that, yes, it is consistent with the Future Gas Strategy, and the release in the Otway region is certainly in the right part of Australia in terms of those depleting gas fields. So it is certainly well positioned vis-a-vis the gas fields that are quickly depleting.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: I know Minister King recently ceded to community pressure to make a modest extension to community consultation on that devastating potential project, but when theoretically—assuming a variety of expected timeframes for approvals—would you expect companies to be pumping gas from these new fields? Ballpark is absolutely fine. There are a number of variables, but do you have a vision for when that would potentially start?

Ms Quinn : It's really difficult for us to be able to make those determinations, because there are various steps and regulatory barriers in there. I'm not sure it's appropriate for us to pre-empt any of those regulatory decisions.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: This decade, though? Do you think it could feasibly happen this decade?

Ms Quinn : It largely depends on the geology and the capability of the enterprises and the regulatory approvals needed, and so there's—

Senator HODGINS-MAY: So there's no guarantee it could actually happen in time for the supposed 2028 shortfall.

Ms Quinn : These projects can take quite a long time. other ones can be much quicker, depending on how they link to existing infrastructure, which goes back to it depending on the geology of the location, the capability of the enterprises and the regulatory regime. I wouldn't want to speculate on a timing.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: I have one more question, and I'll put the others on notice. Minister, will you commit to requiring all companies with gas infrastructure coming offline and already offline in the Bass Strait to properly decommission it and clean up their mess before we allow those same companies to open new gas fields? Is there any commitment there?

Senator Ayres: I might allow the department to outline what the obligations are and what the progress is in relation to those questions. As the secretary outlined, all those obligations must be complied with. The Energy Market Operator is forecasting gas shortfalls for east coast gas in that period from 2027 through to 2029.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: But we're hearing that they very likely won't even be operational by then, and in the meantime—

Senator Ayres: Maybe, but this is a step towards making sure we're doing all the things alongside that reservation strategy to make sure we're delivering for heavy industry in particular, and making sure that Australian gas is there in the Australian interest.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: To your colleagues, then, around the clean up: I've got Victorians contacting me saying they're finding pieces of rigs washing up on the beaches of Victoria. This is going to cost billions of dollars over the next decade. Do you think that's okay, and can you provide an update on that decommissioning, please?

Mr Jeremenko : Under the law, the offshore petroleum industry has an obligation to decommission projects. The costs of that need to be borne by them, not the Australian community. There's been a number of reforms over recent years to further strengthen that decommissioning requirement under the law. Absolutely, it's the case that companies who are making profit, as they should, in investing and extracting the natural resources also have the obligation to pack up when they finish that project, and to do it in an environmentally sustainable way. That is the requirement under the law.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: I suppose it's one thing to have obligations and another thing to put them into practice. Hopefully we don't need this new gas beyond 2030, with the renewable energy transition, and it doesn't just become another corporate handout. Thank you for your time.

Ms Quinn : The regulations are enforced by a regulator—NOPSEMA, who will be here shortly. They have the regulatory obligation to make sure people are complying.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: We'll watch and wait. Thanks.

Senator McDONALD: Ms Quinn, did you consult with the gas industry during your development of the new arrangements with the EPBC legislation and the Greens?
